rv.q: And by the time he and his doubting father (Sifiso Mazibuko) climb up a makeshift wooden mast to generate electricity and faith in the future, this musical has earned its right to pull our heartstrings.
The cast are utterly stellar, and every single actor stands out.

The Royal Shakespeare Company’s production is a soulful, colourful, and uplifting example of how musical adaptation can bring a story to new heights, layering in a new dimension for a pre-existing tale.
Not that many cared on press night and, frankly, neither did I, on my feet and applauding as loudly as I could when the real William appeared at the curtain call.
If this show set out only to inject a little heart into these darkest of times, then it has succeeded.
The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind is incredibly rich and uplifting.

Guided by scraps of knowledge and a sympathetic librarian, he begins to imagine a windmill that could generate electricity and save his community from famine. It is a compelling premise, and Richy Hughes’ book and lyrics ensure that the stakes are always clear.
But if you dislike folksy theatre, this may not suit you.

cn.t: Critics praise this inspiring true story for its vibrant energy and powerful ensemble work, with the intimate staging at @sohoplace effectively immersing audiences in William Kamkwamba's remarkable Malawian community.
